equilibrium-concentrations-s1.title: An ICE table for ammonia
equilibrium-concentrations-s1.text: A sealed 1.00 L vessel starts with 0.500 M N2 and 0.800 M H2 at a high temperature: N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g). At equilibrium, [NH3] = 0.150 M. A student starts an ICE table.

table.caption: Partly completed ICE table (concentrations in M)

equilibrium-concentrations-s2.title: When x is not small
equilibrium-concentrations-s2.text: PCl5 decomposes on heating: PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), Kc = 0.040 at a certain temperature. A sealed flask starts with 0.200 M PCl5 and nothing else. A student writes x2 / (0.200 − x) = 0.040, assumes x is small compared with 0.200, and gets x = 0.089 M.

equilibrium-concentrations-s3.title: Two students solve the same problem
equilibrium-concentrations-s3.text:
For 2 H2S(g) ⇌ 2 H2(g) + S2(g), Kc = 1.0 × 10−6 at a certain temperature. A flask starts with 0.10 M H2S only.

Student P writes the Equilibrium row as [H2S] = 0.10 − 2x, [H2] = 2x, [S2] = x, assumes 2x is small next to 0.10, and writes (2x)2(x) / (0.10)2 = 1.0 × 10−6.

Student Q writes the same Equilibrium row, then drops x everywhere it appears, including the top: (0)2(0) / (0.10)2 = 1.0 × 10−6, and says there is no solution.

items.q: What belongs in the Change row for H<sub>2</sub>?
options: −x

why.correct: The Change row is x times each coefficient, negative for species used up. H₂ has coefficient 3: −3x.
options: Right: three H₂ react for every N₂, so H₂ falls three times as fast.
This ignores the coefficient 3 on H₂.
H₂ is a reactant in a net forward reaction, so it is used up: the sign is negative.
The coefficient multiplies x; it does not divide it.

items.q: Calculate [H<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted [NH₃] directly. 2x = 0.150 M gives x = 0.0750 M, and H₂ falls by 3x.
Value: H₂ falls by 3x, not x. Its coefficient is 3.
Value: x is half of [NH₃], because NH₃ rises by 2x. Use x = 0.0750 M.

items.q: Using the completed ICE table, calculate K<sub>c</sub> for ammonia formation at this temperature.

mistakes.why: Value: [H₂] must be cubed, because its coefficient is 3.
Value: you used the initial concentrations of N₂ and H₂. Use the equilibrium values from the ICE table.

items.q: Why does the Change row use one unknown, x, for all three species?
options: The coefficients fix the ratio of the changes.
The three concentrations change by equal amounts.
x is the equilibrium concentration of each species.
The volume is 1.00 L, so moles and molarity are equal.

why.correct: Species react and form in the mole ratio of the balanced equation, so every change is x times a coefficient.
options: Right: once you know how much N₂ reacted, stoichiometry gives the change in H₂ and NH₃.
They change in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2, not by equal amounts; that is why the coefficients multiply x.
x is the change for a species with coefficient 1. The equilibrium values are Initial + Change.
That makes unit conversion easy but does not explain why a single unknown works.

items.q: Is the student’s small-x approximation valid?
options: No: 0.089 M is about 45% of 0.200 M, far more than 5%.
Yes: x comes out less than 0.200 M.
Yes: K = 0.040 is less than 1.
No: the approximation is not used when the products start at zero.

why.correct: Check the approximation: x / [initial] × 100% = 0.089 / 0.200 × 100% ≈ 45%. Over about 5%, x cannot be dropped and the equation must be solved exactly.
options: Right: the approximation is only safe when x is a few percent of the starting concentration or less.
Being smaller than 0.200 is not enough; x must be negligible next to it (under about 5%).
K < 1 alone does not guarantee x is small. Here K is only moderately small compared with the concentration.
Starting with no products is the usual case for the approximation. It fails here because K is not small enough.

items.q: Solve x<sup>2</sup> / (0.200 − x) = 0.040 exactly (with the quadratic formula) and give [Cl<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the small-x answer, which is invalid here (45% of 0.200). Solve x² + 0.040x − 0.0080 = 0 exactly.
Value: you took the negative root. A concentration cannot be negative; use the positive root.

items.q: Using the exact x, calculate [PCl<sub>5</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the small-x value of 0.089 M. Use the exact x = 0.072 M.
Value: [PCl₅] falls by x as it decomposes. Subtract x from 0.200 M.

items.q: Check: put the exact equilibrium concentrations back into the K expression. What should you get, and what does it confirm?
options: About 0.040, so Q = K.
About 0.089, confirming the approximation was valid.
Exactly 0.200, the starting concentration.
A value less than 0.040, showing the reaction is still going forward.

why.correct: Substituting your answers into the K expression is a quick check: an equilibrium mixture gives Q = K.
options: Right: (0.0717)² / 0.128 ≈ 0.040. Q equals K, so the mixture is at equilibrium.
Substituting into K gives K back, not x. And the approximation was not valid.
The starting concentration is not what the K expression returns.
If the solution is right, Q equals K. A smaller Q would mean an arithmetic error.

items.q: Which student used the small-x approximation correctly?
options: Student P, who drops x just from (0.10 − 2x).
Student Q, who sets each x term to zero because x is small.
Both, because dropping x anywhere gives the same approximation.
Neither, because the approximation works for two-species reactions.

why.correct: The approximation replaces (initial − x) by (initial) when x is tiny. It never replaces x itself by zero.
options: Right: 0.10 − 2x ≈ 0.10 is fine, but x terms standing alone must stay, or nothing is left to solve for.
Setting x to zero on top makes Q = 0, which can never equal K. Only x inside a sum or difference may be dropped.
Dropping x from "0.10 − 2x" changes the value by a few percent; dropping it from "(2x)²x" changes it to zero. They are not the same.
The number of species does not matter. What matters is whether x is small next to the number it is subtracted from.

items.q: Finish Student P’s calculation: find [S<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: (2x)² = 4x², so the top is 4x³. Divide by 4 before taking the cube root.
Value: the top is 4x³, so take a cube root, not a square root.
Value: that is [H₂] = 2x. [S₂] is x.

items.q: How should Student P check that the approximation was justified?
options: Compare 2x with 0.10 M; it is under 5%.
Check that x is positive.
Check that K is less than 1.
Compare x with K; x should be smaller than K.

why.correct: The 5% rule: the amount subtracted (here 2x) should be under about 5% of the starting concentration. If it is, the approximation was justified.
options: Right: 2x = 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M, which is 2.7% of 0.10 M.
A positive x is needed, but it does not show the approximation is valid.
A small K makes the approximation likely to work, but you still verify it with the answer.
x and K are different kinds of quantity; the test compares x with the starting concentration.

items.q: Why was it reasonable to expect x to be small before solving?
options: K = 1.0 × 10<sup>−6</sup> is very small.
The flask starts with no H<sub>2</sub> or S<sub>2</sub>.
H<sub>2</sub>S has a coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation.
The starting concentration, 0.10 M, is less than 1 M.

why.correct: When K is much smaller than the starting concentration terms, little reactant is used, so x is small relative to the initial amount.
options: Right: a tiny K means a reactant-favored equilibrium, so the change from the starting amount is small.
Starting with no products tells you the direction (forward), not how far the reaction goes.
Coefficients appear in the change row but do not decide whether x is small.
The size of the concentration alone does not decide it; the ratio of K to the concentration does.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 50.0 at 450 °C. A flask starts with 0.100 M H<sub>2</sub> and 0.100 M I<sub>2</sub>. Calculate [HI] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: that is x. [HI] = 2x.
Value: you dropped x from 0.100 − x. K is not small here, so take the square root of both sides instead: 2x / (0.100 − x) = √50.0.
Value: that is [H₂] (0.100 − x), not [HI].

items.q: For 2 NOCl(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. A flask starts with 0.50 M NOCl. Using the small-x approximation, calculate [Cl<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: (2x)²x = 4x³. Divide by 4 before taking the cube root.
Value: that is [NO] = 2x. [Cl₂] = x.
Value: the top is 4x³, so take a cube root.

items.q: For CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.56. A flask starts with 0.0500 M CO, 0.0500 M H<sub>2</sub>O, 0.200 M CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>. How should the Change row be written?
options: +x for CO, H<sub>2</sub>O; −x for CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>
−x for CO, H<sub>2</sub>O; +x for CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>
−x for each of the four species
0 for each species, since the four start at nonzero values

why.correct: Compare Q with K before writing the Change row. Q > K means net reverse: the reactant side gains +x and the product side loses −x.
options: Right: Q = (0.200)² / (0.0500)² = 16.0 > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse: reactants form, products are used.
This assumes a forward reaction. Check Q first: Q = 16.0 is greater than K, so the reaction runs in reverse.
Every species cannot decrease; atoms must go somewhere. One side forms while the other is used.
Having all species present does not mean equilibrium. Q = 16.0 ≠ K = 1.56.

items.q: Continue the CO + H<sub>2</sub>O problem (K<sub>c</sub> = 1.56; start 0.0500 M CO, 0.0500 M H<sub>2</sub>O, 0.200 M CO<sub>2</sub>, 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>). Calculate [CO] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: the net reaction runs in reverse, so CO increases: [CO] = 0.0500 + x.
Value: that is x. Add it to the starting 0.0500 M CO.

items.q: Put the steps for finding equilibrium concentrations from K in order.
options: Calculate Q from the starting concentrations and compare it with K to find the direction.
Set up the ICE table with the changes as x times the coefficients, signed for that direction.
Substitute the Equilibrium row into the K expression; simplify if x is small or the expression is a perfect square.
Solve for x, check it (5% rule, or substitute back), and calculate each concentration.

why.correct: Direction first, then the ICE table, then solve and check. The check catches a bad approximation or a sign error.

items.q: In which case is the small-x approximation most likely to be valid?
options: K = 2 × 10<sup>−8</sup>, start at 0.50 M
K = 2 × 10<sup>−1</sup>, start at 0.010 M
K = 5 × 10<sup>3</sup>, start at 1.0 M
K = 1.0, start at 0.10 M

why.correct: x is small when K is much smaller than the starting concentration terms. Always confirm with the 5% check afterward.
options: Right: K is tiny compared with the starting concentration, so x will be a very small fraction of 0.50 M.
K is large compared with the concentration here, so a large fraction reacts.
K > 1 means products are favored; most of the reactant reacts.
K near 1 leaves appreciable amounts of both sides; x is not small.

items.q: For a reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Starting from 0.100 M A, the small-x approximation gives x = 6.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M. Calculate the percent of A that reacts.

mistakes.why: Value: that is x itself. Divide x by 0.100 M and multiply by 100%.

why.correct: x / [A]₀ × 100% = (6.3 × 10⁻³ / 0.100) × 100% = 6.3%. That is just over 5%, so the approximation is borderline; solving exactly is safer.

items.q: For the reaction in the previous calculation, x / [A]<sub>0</sub> came out at 6.3%. What should the student do?
options: Solve exactly; x is over 5% of 0.100 M.
Keep the approximate answer, because 6.3% is less than 10%.
Change K to make x smaller.
Double x to account for the error.

why.correct: If x is more than about 5% of the starting concentration, the approximation is not reliable. Solve with the quadratic formula (or by successive approximation).
options: Right: above about 5%, dropping x from 0.100 − x makes a noticeable error.
The usual threshold is about 5%, set so the error stays within the precision of the data.
K is fixed by the reaction and temperature; you cannot change it to suit the math.
There is no such correction. Solve the full equation instead.

items.q: A flask of A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g) (K<sub>c</sub> small) starts with 0.20 M A instead of 0.10 M A, at the same temperature. Predict each quantity at equilibrium, compared with the 0.10 M flask.

variables.name: [B] at equilibrium
variables.why: With x small, x² ≈ K[A]₀, so doubling [A]₀ raises x (by a factor of √2).

variables.name: K<sub>c</sub>
variables.why: K depends only on temperature, which is unchanged.

variables.name: Percent of A that reacts
variables.why: x grows by √2 while [A]₀ doubles, so x/[A]₀ falls by √2.

variables.name: [A] at equilibrium
variables.why: Most of the extra A remains, because only a small fraction reacts.

why.correct: With K fixed, x ≈ √(K[A]₀). More starting reactant gives more product but a smaller percent reacted.
